title: Indian Contract Act, 1872 — Section 178 (Pledge by mercantile agent)

content.overview: Section 178 provides that where a mercantile agent is, with the consent of the owner, in possession of goods or the documents of title to goods, any pledge made by him, when acting in the ordinary course of business of a mercantile agent, shall be as valid as if he were expressly authorised by the owner of the goods to make the same; provided that the pawnee acts in good faith and has not at the time of the pledge notice that the pawnor has not authority to pledge.
content.glance: Pledge by a mercantile agent in possession with the owner's consent, acting in the ordinary course of business, is valid if the pawnee acts in good faith and without notice of lack of authority.
content.study: Where a mercantile agent is, with the consent of the owner, in possession of goods or the documents of title to goods, any pledge made by him, when acting in the ordinary course of business of a mercantile agent, shall be as valid as if he were expressly authorised by the owner of the goods to make the same; provided that the pawnee acts in good faith and has not at the time of the pledge notice that the pawnor has not authority to pledge. Current-law framing: protects good-faith pawnees dealing with mercantile agents in the ordinary course.

examples.title: Mercantile agent pledge
examples.body: Mercantile agent in possession with consent pledges goods in the ordinary course of business to a good-faith pawnee without notice of lack of authority. The pledge is valid under Section 178.

hypotheticals.question: Mercantile agent pledges goods in the ordinary course to a good-faith pawnee. Is the pledge valid?
hypotheticals.analysis: Yes, if the agent was in possession with the owner's consent and the pawnee had no notice of lack of authority, under Section 178.

enhancement.detailedExplanation: Section 178 validates a pledge made by a mercantile agent who is, with the consent of the owner, in possession of goods or documents of title, when acting in the ordinary course of business of a mercantile agent, provided the pawnee acts in good faith and has not at the time of the pledge notice that the pawnor has not authority to pledge. The pledge is as valid as if the agent were expressly authorised.
examples: Good-faith pledge by mercantile agent in ordinary course is binding on the owner.
